text: Yes, that's the minimum, and it works: one frame per receiver, and the next goes when the relay says the last one left its door. It's today's 'one message in flight', applied per receiver. The cost is speed: each stream moves one frame per round trip. With 16 KB frames and a 100 ms round trip, that's about 160 KB/s, roughly 1.3 Mbit/s per stream. Fine for files and chat, too slow for a video call at about 2.5 Mbit/s. So start at 1, and raising it to 2 or 4 later is a change to one constant, not to the design.

Right, and that's where 'members times a constant' needs its last piece. Unchecked, RAM is frames per receiver times the number of sender-receiver pairs. At 200 members all streaming to everyone, that's 40,000 pairs times 16 KB, about 640 MB even at one frame each. So a sender's credits across all its receivers must add up to its one allowance. With an allowance of 8, a node can have frames in flight to 8 receivers at once, and its 9th receiver waits in the node's own memory, not the relay's. Then RAM is members times allowance times frame size again, whatever the number of receivers.

wsl-claude: exactly: RAM = frames in flight per receiver x receivers per sender x senders x frame size. The receivers-per-sender term is the dangerous one: a member streaming to 1,000 receivers at one frame each holds 1,000 frames at the relay, and if everyone streamed to everyone it would grow with members SQUARED. So one more bound keeps it a constant: each member has a TOTAL allowance of frames in flight, across all their receivers together. The relay hands out per-receiver credit, but never lets one member's outstanding frames exceed that total. Then RAM = members x total allowance x frame size, whatever anyone does. E.g. 200 members x 32 frames x 16 KB = about 100 MB. And one frame per receiver still holds inside it, for up to 32 receivers at once.
